He pare them a prescription for pills, and wrote the direction," One pill to toe taken three nines a day, in any convenient vehicle," The (aridly looked is the dictionary to get at the meming of the prescription. To eat and drink, and sleep—to Le exposid to darkness and the light—to pacel round in the mill of haul, aed turn thought into all MTN- ment of trade—this is not life. In all this, bats poor fraction of the conscientiousness of limminity is awakened, and the sanctities still dumber which make it worth while to be. Knowledge, truth, love, beauty, goodness, faith, alone .n give vitality to the mechanism of existence. THE PEED,"OF EATINO A EIEHICAN HAM AHD TINNED FISH.—On Mond., at the Nantwich Rural Sanitary Autho- : rity. Dr. FOR reported that outbreaks of fever had occurred at Stapeley, Wybunbury, and liaslington, near Crewe. In . Stapelev, almost an entire family were iiimultaneously attacked with scarlet fever. The conditions were so urgent that two more nurses were telegraphed for front Chester, and were yet in attendance. On examination no direct trace of contagion was ascertainable, but in the general sanitary arrangements of the premises, there ma much to find fault with, and the adjoining premiere were of the old condemned cess-pit type, the drainage also being defective, end the water contaminated. It is remarkable in this case (the medical officer goes on to observe) and may be worths, 0 mention here that the Einem in the household occurred in all who were attacked simultaneously after partaking of a meal of American ham. lbus all were seized with the complaint except the baby, which member of the family slow did not eat the ham. The earliest svmptoms, too, were sickness and purging. I am unable to say whether . this may be a coincidence or not. All the eymptoms of the illness were reported to me as those of genuine narlet fever. I have no apprehension myself that well-cooked meat can be the I,CDlsioll of avmotic poisoning, but in regard to the consumption of foreign ham, my &deice would be either to forbear its use, or to be wed armored that before cooking it trout into thin slices, no that the heat may penetrate to every fibre. In Wybonbury a ease of death from typhoid fever has been reported to me. On repairing to the spot I ' toned that the subject was a child who, oddly enough, as following the other case, was wised with diarrhrea after eating heartily of tinned fish. In Abs town of Haslington, . a recent epidemic of typhoid fever posseeses far more in- terest. Here as many as 213 came. fortunately not fatal, have come under the knowledge of my department. The water of the well there he popular use by the affected per- sons affords evidence of much cuoMmination with organic < matter.

A PENNSYLVANIA CAVERN.—A Philadelphia paper gives a description of the recent discovery in Pennsylvania of a .ve which is likely to attract inuch alteration from scientific men. The cave, which is known as the. Crystal Hill Cave," is situated on the limestone reign which eeparatesthe Valley of the P.o. from Cherry Vallee, in Strands Tow.hip, on the south side of the ridge, three miles weat of this place, and five miles from the Delaware Water (iap. It is about 800 ft. above the river level, at what is known as Mosier's Knob, and from it a most picturesque view can be obtained. Lately several men have Woo employed in excavating it, and some interesting discoveries ha.ws been made. The entrance was at first alm.t completely hidden by deposits of clay and animal And vegetable matter, but now it has been opened so that the mouth ie about 18ft-square. The bottom of the cavern was found to he covered with a thick deposit of clay, on the top of which was a deposit, varying in depth, of A dark substance, and oo this is an incrustation of lime which has fallen from the roof of the cave. It is the deposit of rich, dark material that pArticularly interests the scien- lista, and to thisl/r. Leidy and Dr. Porter gave their atten- tion. They found many illdiCAtitilla of the presence in the cove at one time or another of many animals, snare of which were daubtl.s brought there by animals of prey, and others used it for their dens. Among the bones of animals found were the jaw-bones of the racoon, skunk, weasel, beaver, squirrel, porcupine, woodchuck, fox, wild eat, elk, deer, and bison ; the shells of two or more Gird., the bones of wild turkey, and the vertebra of snakes in large quantities Other bones will doubtless reveal the presence of other ani- mals. The most interesting specimens found, however, were the head aid teeth of a gigantic Leaver sCantonsid. Ohio- eusis) and a large peccary s Dicotylus compr.ettel, neither of which have ever been found before in Pennsylvania. ho- aides thee, were found bonne which had been burned and I split—evidently the work of the aborigm., who tiought the I marrow in the bones. Indian relics were also found, among I them being polished bon., needles and bodkins, nest shells,l and fragments of quartz, which had been used as ornaments, a flint spearhead win picked up far back in the cane, im- bedded in the day. How it came there is a mystery, unless I some Indian, entering the rave and finding a will beast there, attacked it. And this Ten-, hurled at the animal. missing in :inn, apel far back into the recess., and there remained until found by the scientists. No other traces of soy kind which would indicate that the portion of the easel in which the spearhead was found had been visited by roan or beast were discovered, and hence the theory as to how it came in the lonely spot. Aspen the lower deposit has not been removed, and it is thought that it will reveal eves more internting facts far the scientists than the middle layer.

-I.I;TIKIMATIONAL WZATIMII Man.—The mast remarkable feature of the United States weather intelligence cousists of a series of charts which are hosed upon the states of the ' 'barometer, the thermometer, and of the weather in different pasts of the globe at ths same instant of time. The work is 100 arranged that the observations both in the old and in the new world, and on the oceins, are taken, not at the same I honrs of local time,but precisely tithe 9111.10 moment, shown at sea by the chronometer—namely, 1 hour 43 min, pm., Greenwich tone; the observerr being at all the instruments at once. The charts on which the observations are used give a synopsis of the atmospheric conditions at the instant. They embrace observations taken in almoet every civilised country north of the equator, as well as observations taken at sea. Hitherto, however: very few observations have been taken for the Pacide Ocean. The publication of these charts was commenced July 1, 1878. The very great value of hemispherical weather maps to meteorologists must be obvious. Their wide and varied significance will begin to be evident by comparing the maps in sue...ion The gime- tine as to the translation of storms from continent to con- tinent, and of the times and directions they may take in such movements ; the displacement. of areas of high and of low barometer; the conditions of temperature, preesure, and wind , direction, existing around the earth ate tined instant, may 1. contrasted ; the distribution and amount of rainfall, and other problems may by such means L. studied. Questions of climatology, and perhaps questions of the character of coming seasons even, may be answered hy the researehes which these charts render practicable. It is an advantage of the method of simultaneous observations that researches by normals, say, monthly mean values, may be made more perfectly than by any other methods of using averages. The shifting positions of the areas of high add low atmospheric premure, with the accompanying changes of temperature, will throw mach light on the changes of weather which oc- curred in the different regions of the northern hemisphere and their rainfall. The comparison of such normals for a given district with theer taken at other districm, annul- lanpusly, give results which may be very different from those arrived at by the see of normals determined in any other manner. Their comparison will show whether and in what manner unseasonable conditions in any district are attended by competwating variations elsewhere. There are many interesting studier as to what sequences may be ex- ',meld to follow any given variations occurring over any region, either in that region or in some other; and how and where the compensating variations occur, and with what I concomitant. or sequencea of meteoric changes. In this way, or by investigations which such study may suggest, I there is goad hope of ultimately gaining knowledge which may greatly benefit thecommercial and agricultural intereata of the worla, IVe cannot doubt that the British Gororn. meat will aid the American Government in this laudable entelyries with all partible cordiaLity and tbortnaghaesa— Toomarisf.

In reply to J. L.," I may state that hate are mid to have been first used by men at the beginning of the fifteenth century. But the batters have • tradition among them, that while St. Clement, the fourth bishop of Rome, woe fleeing from hie persecutors, his feet became blistered, and, to afford him relief, he was Indeced to put wool between his sandals • and the soles of his feet. On continuing his journey, the wool, by the perspiration, motion, and 'tremors of the feet, amounted a uniformly compact eubstance, whkh has since been denomituted felt. When he afterwards settled at Rome, ills mid he improv,l the diecovery; and from this circumstance has beea dated the origin of felting. Hatters in Ireland, and several Catholic countries, still hold their festival on St. Clement's day. Hats, however, are first spoken of in history at the period when Charles VII. made his triumphant entry into Rouen, in the year 1445. In F. Daniel's account of that entry, that prince, he says, asto- nished the whole city by appearing in a hat lined with red Ilk, and eurmounted by a plume of feathers from this entry their general use is dated. In procem of thoe the Clergy also amuined this part of the habit of the laity, but it was looked on as a armt abuse, and several regulations were published forbidding any primt or religious person to appear abroad in a hat without coronet, and enjoining them to keep to the use of chaperoons, made of black cloth, with decent coronet,', if they were poor, they were at leant to have coronets fastened to their hats ; and this upon penalty 01 suspension and excommunication. The use of bats, in. deed, is soil to have been of longer standing among the ecclesiastics of Brittany, by 200 yeare, and especially among the canons ; but these were, in fact, a kind of caps ; whence arose the square cape worn in college's, dm. By the statute of 13 Elia. every persoe above the age of seven years, and goder a certain degree, was obliged on Sundays and holidays to wear, woollen cap, made in England, and finished by some of the fraternity of capper, under the penalty of • 4,1. for every day's neglect. 'llia statute W. repealed 39 Ella. From Stow's Chronicle we learn, that about the beginning of Henry VIII. began the making of Spanish felts in England, by Spaniards and Dutchmen. In the second year of James I. the felt-makers of London obtained aeon' poration, and hired • hall near Christ Church. the king granting them various privileges and liberties for their ammo, Rex, Warringtop 130.—ammtens.

I with pleasure forward the following, in *newer to the question of "M. A." as to the medicinal properties of honey r—lt is a very useful detergent and Aperient, power- /ally dissolving viscid juices, and promoting the expectora- tion of tough plilegnt. In some particular constitutions it los an inconvenience of griping, or of proving purgative which is said to be in some measure prevented by previously boiling the honey. This, however, with all constitutions, is by no means effectual and the circumstance has had so much weight erith the Edinburgh College, that they do not now employ it in any preparation, and have entirely rejected the mella medicate, substituting syrups in their place bet honey is dnubtlese very useful in giving form to diffsrent articles, although there are some individuals with whom it may disagree. In order, however, to obtain the good et' ectn of honey iteelf, it must be used to a considerable extent, and ease. article of diet. 'The following remarkable instances of the good effects of honey in sonaeastlunatic eases are given by lie. Munro in his Medical and Pharmaceutical Chemis- try •—• The late Itr John Hume, one of the commissioners of the sick and harlot the royal navy, was for many years violently afflicted with au asthma. Having taken many medicines without receiving relief, he at last resolved to try the effects of honey, having long had a great opinion of its virtues as a pectoral. For two or three years he ate some minces of it daily, and got entirely free of his esthma, end likewise of a gravelly complaint vrith which he had been long afflicted. About two years after he had recovered his health, when he was sitting one day in the office for the sick and hurt, a person labouring end or a great difficulty of breathing, who looked as if he could not live many days, came to him and asked him by what means he had been cured of his asthma, Iry llama told liiin the particulars of his own case, and mentioned to him the means by which he had found relief. For two years after he heard nothing of this person, who was • stranger to him, ant bad seemed so bad that he did not imagine that he conld have lived nany days, and therefore had not even uked him who he was; , be, at the end of that period, man seemingly in good lmalth, and decently &owed, came to the sick and hurt office, and returned him thanks for his cure, which he as. enrol him had been entirely bronght about by the free use of honey." E. Jac..., St. Helens.

L'S, desires, on the emendating of the thirteenth annual Trade-union Congress of Great Britain, to express its profound sympathy with you In the noble work you are doing for the bettering of the' condition of the wage.workers of Great Britain and of the world, and our unqualified admiration of the in,thods used to carry your projects into exemstion. Others expremed doubts as to the support Accrington would receive in the event of a etrihet and, after a lengthened discussion, a resolution to abandon the strike for tbe present was passed by about thirty votes to five. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.

Thu week the clergy and representative laymen. of the Established Church have been sitting in congress at Leicster. Among the nubjecte la ought beforothe Congo.e for diroussion were the relations subsisting between (Porch and ate and the deeirs.bility of a return of Diantere to the bosom of the Church. The apoeches, both clerical and lay, betray that the yvowth and smear, of the free churches of the venally have had their iullance in promoting a spirit of inquiry and a yearning ftr greater freedom witbin the E.tab• liahnieut itself. While retaining all the old love for the glided trappings, dignities and dintinaces born of the connection between the Church and the State, there it a vrinh undoubtedly growing in the Church 1 to be rid of Parliamentary control. He would like them to say, when the Church was established, by what statute, and at what period of her history. (Hear, hear.) After s short speech from the boo. member for Nonvoce, the Holm adjourned at ten o'clock. •

div.head: • MR. J. G. McMINNIES, M.P., ON NONCONFORMITY.
div.p: • MR. J. G. McMINNIES, M.P., ON NONCONFORMITY.

Mr. McMinnies,M E., prmided at a large meeting held in the Exchange Hall, Blackburo, on Monday Evening, on the iocmaion of the delivery of a lecture on the Hiss of Evan- geliml Nonconformity, by the bee. R. W. Dale, of Birming- ham. In introducing the lecturer, Mr. Mcklinnien, who was wermly received, mid. I euppow that the idea that striken us firet and perhaps most etrongly in connection with thew lectures is the difference between Nonconformity of our titer and Nonconformity at the time treated of by the lecturer. At that time Nonconformity wee struggling Mill great dis- couragement for bare existenee, and emn in the paliniest dam of that period not many great and not many mighty men were numbered in its ranks, although at one time perh ips the greatest men of the day were to. It was every- where spoken against. For the most part, the people who professed our opinions were persecuted sometimes to the death. oftener to exile and it wan through great tribuLdion that they emured for on them civil and religious privileges that we possess at the present day (Applaune.) An reg ads Nonconformity, however, in these particulars. everything in now changed. Nonconformity in now a great power in the State. (Cheers.) We have been assured by the lent Stat.- man of our was going to say of the age—(applausel that Nonconformists were an important element in that great political movement which recently destroyed one of the must powerful Governments we have seen in our don—s tiorernment strong in its Parliamentary majority, and ntrong in the affections of the Crown. I nay we have seen Nonconformity one most important element in the movement which struck that tiovemment to the ground. (Cheers) Instead of struggling for nere existence Non- conformists now-a-days Naked for perfect emielity with every man and every other denomination. (Hear, hear.) Not nnly so, but they are claiming and very likely will emceed in their Aims before very bong in putting sn end to all connection between the State and any sect of religionists (Hear, hear.) But whilst there is this increase of power, there is no doubt it brings with it an increase of renown- bility. (Hear, beer) Nonconformists ought to understand their principles and ought to be resolute in maintaining them. (Hear, hear.) We ought not to arbnit any inferiority to anyone else on account of our religious opinion, but whilnt we am self-assertive in this manner we ought to ad- vocate our opinions with a certain amount of meekness and in such a way that we shall not give offence to reasonable men who may differ from us (Applanee.) Well, now, ladies and gentlemen, I have been spending a good that of tine. lately, and Ism hound On admit, at very disreputable hours, In an assemble the chairman of which is called the Speaker, although he speaks very infrequently and very briefly. (Laughter.) tom going to imitate that gentleman to-night, and shall not el..nri between you and the lecturer. I need not commend his addrem to your cordial atb-ntion. I have no doubt he wi I take eare of that, and I hope and believe at the end of thin eveningin engagement we shall all find ourselves better and wiser men and wotnen. (Applause.) After remponding to a vote of thanks to himeell, the lecturer proponed a aimilar compliment to the chairman, and remarked that the queetion of disestablishment had had too exclusive a piece in the 'minds of Nonconformiets for man• yearn part, and he urged them to remember that large nomhers of the early Nonconformistr were quite willing that the civil magietrite should render varied fortns of service to the Church of Christ. 'the Church, he added, wan a great innlitution for the conversion of mankind, anil only as they brought it into harmony with Christ's thought could Obey hope for the triumph of the Gospel over the human race. He afterwards mid he trusted to see great things aye complished by the present House of Commons. Ile thought Ohs Government had done womlern in the session which had just closed, and in the next and the following seesions be wee prepared to em Liberals standing shoulder to shoulder resolved to carry, notwithstanding all obstruction, the great measures that would be brought forward.—CounFillor Boernum seconded the motion, which IVA. carried.

In responding. Mr. McMneurns. after acknowledging the compliment and expreesinc his appreciation of the lecture, remarked : Mr. Irate has said that he hoped that Pailiament will pass some very good meamtres during the next one, two, or three sessions. I have no doubt at all that very good measures will o• propnsed to Parliament. I believe that the I better these measures ate the more difficult It will be to pasre! them through both Houses, and I should not he atoll sur- prised if the Prime Minister has to App.t to the country upon some one or two of those measures. It will depend ' upon the electors of the country whether those measnres—if they Are very good ones—should be forced through an unwilling Parliament no that you see it is quite possible that you may have something tode in connection with those measures to which Mr. Hale has alluded. (Applause.) The proceedings then terminated.

On Thursday afternoon about soo notice, lamed by separate bondholders,and representing about £38.000, which Win. Gourley, rho late clerk to the Onwaldivostle Local Board, embezzled, were served upon each and every member of the Oswaldtwistle Local Boant since the formation of the Board up to the last election. 'I he notice Speeifirei net. in pursuance of the Public Health Act, each of the members who have sat on the board will be nerved with a writ from all the bondholders after the expi- ration of one month—first, to recover from each the soma paid to Gourley, and which he embeezled ; second, to re- cover the sem and sums. and damages, with such other damages as the law allows, bectuse the Raid members war. ranted the 'ceders that Gourley was duly authorised.to re- rely. the sums, whereas he was not so authorised, and the loans had been repudiated by the tioard ; third, because the members neither individually nor collectively were Authorised to receive the some; fourth, because the mem- bers had warranted that they were not authorised to borrow the sums: fifth, because they negligently permitted GoutlaV to borrow the moneys, and by Rationing and authorising the , meal of the board to be affixed to securities tor inoneys se bocowed without due investigation, and by their negligence in permitting Goorlay to have exclusive puesession of the seal, enabled him fraudulently to obtain the moneys. Thia affects 20 members of the board, including the present clerk. The affair has caused considerable excitement amongst the members and the public generally.

The following letter from a gentleman to Galveston. wbo formerly kept a shop in Cburch-streot, to. 10 .1.5,., has been received by • gentleman now residing in this town : "lialveston, Texas, Aural IS. 11050. My dear, Every thing that lam worth to-day 1 owe to teetotalism and I have made • few dimes since I came to Texas. I ant doing wall, exceeding weil,—sonse of my rival. my diabolically well,—for 0 is an arttele of belief with there that lay s6ccese comes of • league I bare entered into with my old enemy the devil. I started buminess here 21 ymrs ago. watt a very small capital, and without • friend on whom assistance to rely. I was. in fact, unknowing and uuknown My business too, selling roasted coffee, was. on.. one for people. All bought green coffee and roasted it in the oven or the Irving pan. I roestel thero aacke of 130Ibe each 5 week, and that •ell ample for my traits Now I ern roasting over 2,0001ba. of coffee a weer, and I have advice to say of the arrival 01 01,0 wharf front New York tot a new roamer the latest and rnoel approved principle which will cost roe 300 dollars (1.401. I have alm bought a new engine and boiler, and in • few days I shall have capacity for roasting 10 sanks a day. Every man, elm was in the bminess when I started, ILO "bonito." My chief rival, an Englishman, who founded the first coffee. rouging businms in this city, is working for meter eighty dollars (SIT) per month. To Ciud be all the glory. Ikanq imagine that I au, religious. lam not. I never go to a place of worship. The last time I attended Divine service was on Christmas Eve, when I went with a crowd to wit,m the performance at the Catholic church. You pee, I cannot hold with the hare and at the non,. time rue with the hounds, for I have fallen into the habits of the Tssana, and I open my shop on Sunday mornings from 5.30 toy, lii, the best of business we have through the week' a raffling, I lively time. I make my expense. out of my Sunday busi-1 nees. You will say. ..1111Ca bad ''; aucl not mid w ben L Met came here, and I curtest considerably, but I fell ioto the way, though much against my will, for, apart from its re-1 !igloos emaciation& I like one day of rest in a week, and it is necessary, working, as we to, almost every hour that God smds—opening our etorea at 5.30 every morning, and keeping open till eight every night. By the time English grocers are taking down their shuttem we have seen the ' the busiest. part of the day. After eight in the morning trade drags slowly along unlit sundown. for you must know • that the hmt Juring the day is intolerable, utterly unsuited to Englishmen. And this leads me to your question aneut Texas as a suitable coentry to emigrate to. of have done well, soda,,, now doing well, much beater than I could do in England, and also better than I ever Loped to do in Texas ; but still I am of the opinion that Texoo is the worst country in the world that an Englishman can emi- grate to. The climate is terribly eevere: the heat of summer and the sharp biting north winds of winter cause sickness without cessation. You would have hard work to find a location that would give your living where chills and fever are not the normal condition of all who live there. l'arming does not pay. If the inmates of the jails and workhouses of England were 1,4 0,, the fond that the Tex. farmer is compelled to live on, there would In an insurrection. (I have just received a letter from Peter Car- ter, in which ha orders 45Ibs of tea, and he I do not think I shall settle in Te.s. I shall mll out the first chmere, as provisions are so high that we cannot oaks much.") labouring men are wretelndly paid, and looney mauy mses are not pail at all, for you must know there ie no law by which a workingman can compel Iris master, if his master ben farmer, to pay hint wages. A man', life and property are not safe, as yon reckon safety. A human life is of far less value in the eye of the Tex,, law, and in the em,, of the Texans, than im the life of a horse or 000 n,. There arena facilitim for educating children. The free echo.' system, of which so much is said by the emigration agents, exist, only in the fertile brains of those agents. L.d,it is true, is cheap, but what with the drought and the cotton worm. and the caterpillars, farmers make mighty little out at their land. There are meowho hold hundred's of acres of Texas lands, and do as they will they cannot raise money to pay the taxm 012 their lands. Thonaands of acres change hands every year Zeman kis.) an acre; and to day am. can buy out a large number of emigrant. at 50 cents on the dollar ; that is, for land that cost them 900 dolLars per acre as prairie they would be very glad to take 150 dollars per acre, with imprommenla thrown in. THE BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL ON CHURCH AND DISSENT.

........--. ...., ....---._. At the Chureh Conferees, an Wednesday, the subject for di.useion in the evening woe "The respormibility of the Church towarde dissent, with special regard to home reunion." The Bishop of Peterborough presided, end there we.. crowded audience. The Rev. Profeesor Plumptr.„ vicar of Bickley, Kent, who read a paper on the subject, said he confeeeed the prospects of home reunion, inths sense in which be had to deal with it, seem neither very definite nor very bright. Earl Nelson rmd a paper on the UM .bect. ljhe Bimini. or Liveammtsaid • Dimwit frordthe Estab- tithed Church of Engleud is a huge standing fact. The collector of statistics, Who makes notee about everything, will tell you that there are scores of religiouadenominittions is England beside the Episcopal, and that their members may be ;numbered by millions. English Proteetant dissent . asr%et"arfe"weatonda itt tit ttu:',l7,l`,7:`,lr—t 'a' itry*co'W n eoNLw- lion of the pruble, is ehort and simple. I believe that the first seeds of diesent were sown by the .rrow intolerance of the Church in the days of the Stuarts. The wretched attempt to produce uniformity by fines and penaltiee and imprisonment "drove wise men almost mad," and made them my "Con any good thing come out of a Church which eangtiom loch things?' I believe, secondly, that' the utter deadness and apathy of the Charrh in the last century did even more to drive men and women out of our pale than the intArance of the ' Stuarts. Bishops who ....lonely neglected their di.eses„ and were everything that bishops ought not to be, parochial clergymen who did -nothing for Boas, preached no gospel, and Hoed tembly worldly lives—these unhappy , repreeeitatives of our Church filled the country. These weep the real founders of diment, and caused halPthe die- 1 serfliog chapels to he built in the land. I declare my own firm conviction that if the bishops and clergy of the last i century had done their duty, and ungferstood their times as , .. well as meny do now, an immense proportion of Englith nonconformity would never have existed, and John Wceßy I and his companiors would never have seceded from the ' Church of F.ngland. We reap what oar forefathers sowed, and It is no use to complain. In short, Church apathy has created English nonconformity, and to speak angrily and contemptuously of these whom we oureelvm have made dieeenters Is, to pay the least, most uojust. On the one hand, I have not the 'lightest sympathy with those who regard dissent . an evil, and only evil, and would hand Nonconformiste over to the ' " uncovenanted mercies" of God. I believe this to be an ' entirely untenable position. I shall never henitate to declare ' my conviction that in thousands of parishes disseeters have ' done an imnienee amount of ratintual good. They have ' Ripened the Church's " lack of service." They have brought to Christ myriad. who were perishing in ignorance and .in. They have taught the elements of Christianity to multitudes who would otherwiee have died without Goal and without hope ; and I hold, with the great Apostle of the Gentiles, "if Christ is preached I rejome, yea and I mill , rejoice." Above all I cannot forget that remarkable ;image in the gospel when John said to our great Master : "We saw one casting out devils in Thy name, and he followed not with as and we forbad hitn, Leconte he followeth not us. But Jesus said Forbid him not . for there is no man which ' shall doe miracle in aly name that can lightly speak evil of Me. For he that in not against ue is on our part." ' In short, when I look at the more of infidelity, ' heathenism, and immorality which exists in the world, ' I meet and will thank God for the work done by ' Trinitarian Dissenters. The eneeny is coming upon us like I a flood; I welcotne any volunteer who tights ou our side, ' however strange and rough his nniform may be. Human ! nature le like a wreck one sandbank ; I welcome any oars- ' man who will help to launch the lifeboat and rescue souls ' from a watery grave. On the other hand it is vain to deny ' that the inconveniences, not to say the evils, arising from ' English dissent are very many and very great. The ' divisions of Christian. are alwaya an immense seerr, of i weakness to the whole cause of Christ in the world. An I enormous amount of tit., money, awl energy is wanted on separate tnachinery and organimtion which would be laved if we were one mile,' body. We mpply the infidel with . argnment which it is extremely difficult to refute. "When you can agree atnong youreelves," lie eats, "it will be time enough for me to believe." Collisione are continually arising between church and chapel, and especially in small parishes., where either it trly thinks its interests are in danger. The common mime of Christian educa- tion takes damage all over the country from the morbid fear of many that distinct Feliciaos teaching will injure Choir own particular denominations. Above all the eenne- -1.3 bitter crusade of liberationists spinet the Establish. I ment, which, If socceseful, would only piranha) the rural • districts and do its promoters no good, is rapidly creating.. breach between Episcopalians end their Goals which, will never he heeled. All these I eay are evils, grevious evils, and I pity the man who han not even to err them, or, Seeing then, does not long to devise means by which they may be leseened or removed. 'rm. brings me at last to the crux of the whole subject: Can nothing be done to Improve the relations of the Church and dissent? The present state - of thing, is painfully unnatisfactory. The ['Melons of Chriallute who hold such an immenee amount of truth in common about the Bible, the Trinity, the Atonement, the work of Christ, anti the work of the Holy Spirit, about t repentance, and conversion, and faith, and holiness, and ' heaven and hell, and resurrectionsed jedgment—these divi- ' sions, I say, are scandalous and deplorable. They are enough i to make an angel weep. Can nothing be done to ameliorate the existing condition of things and bring us closer together? I will offer a few plain suggestions Dona the standpoint of a Churchman. 1. For one thing we should always remember that we most draw a broud line of dis- tinction letween disamiters and dissenters. If we suppose, for, example, because some wild men are incemantly telling the public then the Established Church lea ILlivlon which ought to be destroyed, or that all the prayer-b.hs ought to be burned, or that the union of Chunk and State lean adul- terous connection, or that all clergymen ought to be dripped of their endowments and turned into the streets, or that Anglican minister/ are mere serfs and slaves who are paid out of the taxes—lf. I say, we suppose because some dis- Meters talk this rabbish that all dissenters agree with them, we are quite mistaken. I believe, on the contrary, that the vast majority of serious God-fearing nonconformists have no sympathy with this kind of language, and thoroughly dislike it. Although attached to their own chapel., they heve no wish to quarrel with ills Church, and are willing to" think and let think." 'The empty tube always make most noise. We must not condemn all dissenters on account of the extravegant words of a rabid minority. 2 For another thing we most cultivate the habit of treating die. ' meters with kindness, courtesy, and cormiderstion. Let as ' not deal with them as the Jew, did with the Samaritans. I am firmly convinced, after studying diseent carefully for about 40 years, that many dissenters are what they are from downright ignorance. Cradled and mimed in the midst of nonconformity, taught from their earlieet years to see all religion through the spectacles of the chapel, trained from their Youth to reed nothing but non-episcopalim literature, accusiorned every Sunday to been nothing but a Methodist, m Baptist, or Independent sermon, they often know nothing 1 whatever of the Church of England, its worship, its history, it. theology, its claims to attention. In Mort, they are almost entirely ignorant of the communion from which they keep aloof. And when you add troll this the painful fact that the only parochial incumbent whom they have known has sometimes not adorned his profeasion, and has seemed cobs a man determined to know everything except "Jesus Christ and Him crucified," we really mud not le eurprised wet the prejudices of dissenters, and most make great allowances. In short we must deal gently with them, and not forgot the circumstances under which their position was first taken up. 3 For another thing we meat not waste time and energy on the pleasant but quixotic idea that we can ever bring a wholesale reunion of church and dissent. lam sorry to throw cold water on the charitable plans of some of my brethren. I freely ad- mit that nothing is itnp.mible. But of all improbable and unlikely things I see none more improbable and unlikely than a fusion as,l amalgamation of Methodista, Indepen- dents, and litptiets with the Chnrch of England. Whatever rnay happen in imlated came, it is not reason to suppose that trained and educated dimenting ministers, as a rule, will ignore their own todern aml eeek to be re-ordained. SINGULAR PROCEEDINGS IN BANKRUPTCY.

At the ft. Helens County Court, on Thursday last, before T. R. Collier, Esq., deputy judge, an action was hrought by Mr. Edward Johnson, the Mayor of St. Helene and proprietoe of the Swan Lave Collieries, against Mange. Joh• Simpson and Compony, coal merchants, Stockport and Liverpool, to recover the sum of £32 138. 6d., being ft balanm of no account for good. nekl anl delivered. Mr. Swift appeared for WO plaintiff ; and Mr. McEirio, of Mao- cheeter, for the defendant.. Mr. Swift, in opening the use, mid that the plaintiff was a colliery prolirietee and coal merchant, owning milierim Of I Swan Lane, Ifinilley, and Golliorne, awl having an office in St. Helens. In the early part of 1879, the defendants nom- roenced taking coal from the plaintiff. They obtain.' • quantity in the month of February, and a further quantity in March. The coal obtained M thew two montla amounted In val. to £3O 12e. ld. The defendants' solicitor had given , him notice that they relied for their defence ma a ...Nai- -1 lion obtained by the defenchints under the Bankruptcy Act which exonerated them fluor the present plaint. When the tintt come for the payment of the plaintiff's account, he got I• polite intimation that the parties were insolvent, nod that he might take what he could get. The defendant.' elicitor , alleged that, on the 29th of March, the defendants filed, in I the Stockport County Court, a petithio for liquidation of their affairs by arr.gement or COMPOSIIIOII with their l creditors, and at a meeting held on the 10th of April a i resolution was passed accepting of a composition of lie. tkl. in the potted, payaltle ho instalments. It was said that plaintiffs alum was included in the list of creditors,and the plaintiff ha. been duly paid £6 18s. 7d., beiog a composition ,of Ss. 6d. in the pound upon a sum of £39 12e. 1,1. It Pile I adtnitted by the pleadings on the 29th of March, 1879, the 'defendants did owe Mr. Jolgimn the eum of £35 12a. Id., I and the ar4unt for which he (the plaintiff) claimed was precisely tlaMifference between that £39 12., Id. and £l3 18s. 7,1. ineotinued M the defendant's solicitor'e special nom of defence. Supposing his friend the defearlant's solicitor proved his special. defence in the form Le had pleaded it, then—prinut Pick—hit epecial defence would be the answer to the claim. The point was title' the defendant. might nearly be bankrupt, and petition for liquidation of his affairs by arrangement, and after they twA been die- charged by force of the Bankrupt Act, it was competent for them to recognise and revive the debt by matters subse- quent. At comm. law if a person wished to deal with another he might in consideration of the credit he was going hi receive, more into a promise m contract not only to pay for what he was going to receive, but also enter into a con- tract to pay something over and above that in payment of the old debt, as an inducement to the vendor Li give the desired credit. He might call their attention to a recent case decjded on that point, nix., Jakenian V. Cooke, 4 Chan. ifivision, page 20 L. J. reporte. 'That caw was heard and determined upon the 1911, of November, 1978, where a debtor, aftor having obtained rn order of diecharge under the Bankruptcy Act, 1869, promises torn new and valuable comideration to pay the debt which by virtue of section 49 had been rel.sed by discharge, an action laid against hint for the amoont of the debt. The defemlante, on the 29th of March, petitioned for liquidation, and during the peralancy of thew proceedingn the defendant tried to get coal from Mr. Johnson evrn promises to pay £lO a inoML towards the liquidation of the old debt and prompt payment for all goods he received, and upon that new cause and consideration the plaintiff can entitled to recover the original debt, as per the decision of Jakenun and Cooke. Upon the 14th May defendant's agent called upon Mr. John- son at St. Helens and told him that he had authority to say that if It, would let them have coal monthly they (detenti- on.) would pay off the old account by instalments of £lO a month and in order that he (the plaintiff( might make no mistake, he wrote a letter to the defendants at their 9000 k. port °flee &tying what their representative had told him. In consequence of the lettere which passed betweeo then the plaintiff gave credit to the defendants nd sup- plied them with coal when required. Remittances ran. regularly every month for the coals that had been received, but no money in payment of the old deht,and in consequence the plaititiff wrote to the defendant saying be iv. surprised to find that no money had been sent. Afterward, in came- quence of receiving uo money ill settlement of the old account, the plaintiff stopped the supply of coals, and the present action ensued. For the plaintiff Mr. Swift called

Alexander Hutchinson, residing at 35, Cicely.st., pool, who stated that he was formerly in the employment of John Slum/ton and Co., the defendants in the action, and remembered their going into liquidation. Shortly before the I petition for liquidation he intnsluced hit firm to Mr. John- son, the plaintiff, and an account was opened through wit. DIMS intervention. The liquidation commenced at the end of March or beginning of April, 1879, and he believed ' the transactions with Mr. Johnson bad commenced only within the two predating mouths. Ile saw Mr.Seep- von early in May of lag year. and told him that many of the customer. preferred Mr. Johnson's COMS. Mr. Johnson having declined to serve any more coal, Mr. Simpson asked witness to go to Mr. Juhrwon and say that they would pay the uld account in full, if Mr. Johnson wool,i re-open the account. This witness did, and an account was again opened. Witness would have paid in the ordinary course had not lee been countermanded by one of the tirm.:—Crosas examined by Mr. McEwin, witness sahl that Mr. Simpson had never repudiated the transaction between him (wiroyerd and Mn. Johnson, and he had not been discharged on that account.

Mr. Edward Johnson then gave °violence, and mid that st preeent there was owing to him £32 13e. 8,1. Ile cor- roborated the statement mode by the last witness in respect to the opening of the new account, and added that he would never have sopplhod any coal of a promine to pay the old 000)01 1)0)1 not been made.

Croes-eatimined by Afr: !deErein, witness said that he bad not supplied blotto.on with coal eince theclose of the liquida- tion, esupt under the new arrangament. Mn. Ilektwin, for the def.ce. said there was nothing in writing to rely upon, the only evidence of an arrangement being the statement of Hutchins., which was contradicted by the delendants. If bin Honour thought he WAS bolllld o go on with the case he would put Simpson ill the box, and it would In tor his Honour to say which of the two men

Honour said that he might call the defendant, John Simpson, who stated that what the witness Hutchin- son had said was not wholly the truth. At the time he railed he sent for every agent to come and eon him, and amongst other agents Hutchinson came. He told hint that he should like to see Mr. Johnson paid. Ile distinctly told Hutchinson that heshould not promise the plaintiff anything. Witnesa handed up to his I tonour • bank book, elating that he wished hint to see that at the time he had money in the bank to pay the plaintiff. Ilia Honour No, I don't want to see it.
..-..--. . Mr. Sw if t : If that is the cape you ought to be ashamed of youaelf to fail in L 13,0110, and hare& lot of surplus money in the hank.

His Honour I think that nn the authority of the case !cited before me, the plaintiff is entitled to recover. It is an entirely new debt in consideration of the promise, and the , plaintiff it entitled to my judgment. . . . . . . . .
The defendants' solicitor gave notice of appeal, and his Honour agreed that in the meantime his judgment be sus- pended.

Tea TYPOPTANT APPLICATION PROM Tee LICNNSID VICPCALLIIPS.-11 will he remembered that at the previous session*, Mr. Fletcher, seer., at Northwich, applied that the Bench would recommend that the townships of Halton sod Weston should be doctored populous places within the meanirg of the Licensing Act, thus equalising the time at which the publican. and beersellers in the entire Petty Sessional would have to clues their houses. The Bench then . stated that they would give the mutter their careful con. eideration. Mr. J. R. Fletcher now appeared en behalf nl Ns brother (who was not able to be .present) as the repre- ,entatim of the licensed victuallers.—Mr. Daglish mid that he and his fellow magistrate. had had • meeting to consider the application, and they were not inclined to make the re- . commendations salted for to the Liedosing Committee in the cam of either township—Mr. Fletcher mid he did not know whether the proceedings would he carried still further, after the decision of their worships. He should like to comider • the matter, and then he, or his brother, would report to Mr. Ashton, the magistrates' clerk, their decision. . .• ' " ' •

Joan Lmrs.—The jury Bete for the various townships were laid before the Bench, and sanctioned, there being no objection to them.
